prompt: Does top-k filtering affect the reported probability of the chosen token?
title: Top-k Filtering and Token Probabilities
body:
When a language model samples text, it often applies top-k filtering to discard unlikely candidates before picking a token. This truncation leaves only the top $k$ tokens and sets the rest to zero probability.

Look at the bars in

```rh-diagram
{"version":1,"diagram":{"title":"Full softmax and top-3 sampling","caption":"The kept tokens originally hold 0.8 of the probability. Divide each kept probability by that total.","kind":"bar-chart","unit":"%","variant":"grouped","categories":["on","near","under"],"series":[{"label":"Full softmax","values":[50,20,10]},{"label":"Top-3 renormalized","values":[62.5,25,12.5]}]}}
```

to see how filtering shifts the relative weights of the remaining choices.

Because the total probability must sum to one, the remaining probabilities are scaled up through a process called renormalization.

The reported probability of the chosen token changes because it is divided by the sum of the kept probabilities rather than the full distribution sum.

prompt: Does top-k filtering affect the reported probability of the chosen token?
title: Top-k Filtering and Token Probabilities
body:
Top-k filtering truncates a model's probability distribution by keeping only the $k$ most likely tokens and setting the rest to zero.

To ensure the remaining probabilities sum to one, the kept values undergo renormalization, dividing each by the sum of the survived probabilities.

This mechanism directly alters the relative weights among the retained candidates.

```rh-diagram
{"version":1,"diagram":{"title":"Full softmax and top-3 sampling","caption":"The kept tokens originally hold 80% of the probability. Divide each kept probability by that total.","kind":"bar-chart","unit":"%","variant":"grouped","categories":["on","near","under"],"series":[{"label":"Full softmax","values":[50,20,10]},{"label":"Top-3 renormalized","values":[62.5,25,12.5]}]}}
```

When these modified values are reported as token probabilities, they no longer match the original softmax output from the network layer.

The probability assigned to the chosen token increases because the probability mass of the discarded tokens is redistributed across the survivors.

prompt: Does top-k filtering affect the reported probability of the chosen token?
title: Top-k filtering and token probabilities
body:
When a language model samples text, it often applies top-k filtering to restrict choices to the $k$ most likely next tokens.

This process discards all other vocabulary items by setting their logits to negative infinity before computing probabilities.

```rh-diagram
{"version":1,"diagram":{"title":"Full softmax and top-3 sampling","caption":"The kept tokens originally hold 80% probability. Renormalizing divides each by 0.8.","kind":"bar-chart","unit":"%","variant":"grouped","categories":["on","near","under"],"series":[{"label":"Full softmax","values":[50,20,10]},{"label":"Top-3 renormalized","values":[62.5,25,12.5]}]}}
```

Because the discarded tokens carried some probability mass, the remaining probabilities no longer sum to one.

To fix this, the model performs renormalization by dividing each kept token's probability by the sum of all surviving probabilities.

Consequently, the reported probability of the chosen token increases compared to the raw softmax output. This mathematical scaling ensures valid probability distributions are passed to the sampler.

prompt: What does predicting the mean give as a regression baseline?
title: Predicting the Mean as a Baseline
body:
When evaluating a regression model, we often compare its performance against a simple baseline. A common choice is predicting the mean of the target values for every single input observation.

This constant prediction ignores all features and yields a horizontal line on a plot.

```rh-diagram
{"version":1,"diagram":{"title":"A constant mean baseline","caption":"Illustrative values; the geometry shows the stated relationship.","kind":"coordinate-plot","x":{"label":"Sample","min":1,"max":5},"y":{"label":"Target","min":0,"max":10},"series":[{"label":"Targets","kind":"scatter","points":[{"x":1,"y":2},{"x":2,"y":4},{"x":3,"y":5},{"x":4,"y":7},{"x":5,"y":7}]}],"annotations":[{"kind":"reference-line","label":"Mean prediction of 5","axis":"y","value":5}]}}
```

The height of this line is the arithmetic average of all targets, which minimizes mean squared error. Look at the reference line in the plot to see how residuals sum to zero around it.

Any useful model must achieve a lower error than this naive strategy.

body:
When building a regression model, we often start with a simple baseline that ignores the features and always predicts the same value.

The most common naive predictor is the average target value across the training dataset.


Notice how the horizontal reference line cuts across the scatter points at a constant level.

This constant prediction minimises the mean squared error, making it a robust reference point for evaluating more complex models.

If a sophisticated machine learning model cannot outperform this simple average, it fails to capture meaningful patterns in the data.

Thus, the mean baseline establishes the minimum performance bar for any regression task.

title: Confusion matrix with exact counts
body:
Consider a binary classifier evaluated on 100 items. The confusion matrix records how many predictions match the true class.

The matrix below shows the exact counts: true negatives (TN) = 50, false positives (FP) = 10, false negatives (FN) = 5, true positives (TP) = 35.

```rh-diagram
{"version":1,"diagram":{"title":"Confusion matrix counts","kind":"heatmap","rowLabel":"Actual","columnLabel":"Predicted","columns":["Negative","Positive"],"rows":[{"label":"Negative","cells":[50,10]},{"label":"Positive","cells":[5,35]}],"range":{"min":0,"max":50}}}
```

Rows correspond to actual classes, columns to predicted classes.

From these numbers, precision = TP/(TP+FP) = 35/45 ≈ 0.78 and recall = TP/(TP+FN) = 35/40 = 0.875. These metrics summarise classifier performance.

title: Understanding a Confusion Matrix with Exact Counts
body:
Consider a binary classifier that labeled 100 instances.  The concrete counts are: 50 true negatives, 10 false positives, 5 false negatives, and 35 true positives.

```rh-diagram
{"version":1,"diagram":{"title":"Confusion matrix for binary classifier","caption":"Counts of true/false positives and negatives for a sample model.","kind":"heatmap","rowLabel":"Actual","columnLabel":"Predicted","columns":["Negative","Positive"],"rows":[{"label":"Negative","cells":[50,10]},{"label":"Positive","cells":[5,35]}],"range":{"min":5,"max":50}}}
```

A confusion matrix arranges these numbers in a 2×2 grid. Rows show the actual class, columns the predicted class.

The top‑left cell (TN) holds correct negatives, top‑right (FP) holds negatives mis‑predicted as positive, bottom‑left (FN) holds positives missed, and bottom‑right (TP) holds correct positives.

These four cells let you compute performance metrics.  For example, precision = TP/(TP+FP) = 35/(35+10)=0.78, and recall = TP/(TP+FN) = 35/(35+5)=0.88.  The matrix thus makes the classifier’s errors explicit.

diagrams.caption: Counts of true/false positives and negatives for a sample model.

title: How “sat” attends to the sentence
body:
In self‑attention each token acts as a **query** that gathers information from all tokens, including itself. The strength of each gathering is the **attention** weight.

For the word “sat” we compute a query vector, compare it to every key vector, and turn the similarities into probabilities that sum to one. These probabilities tell us which words influence the representation of “sat”.

```rh-diagram
{"version":1,"diagram":{"title":"Attention weights from “sat”","caption":"Arrows show how much each token contributes to the representation of “sat”.","kind":"token-links","source":["the","cat","sat","on","the","mat"],"target":["the","cat","sat","on","the","mat"],"queries":[{"index":2,"weights":[0.05,0.45,0.05,0.1,0.05,0.3]}],"normalized":true}}
```

The diagram shows that “cat” (0.45) and “mat” (0.30) dominate, while the two “the” tokens and “sat” itself contribute only a little.

Thus the model focuses on the noun that performed the action and the location where the action happened.

prompt: When the word sat attends to the sentence the cat sat on the mat, which words matter most?
title: Self-attention weights for sat
body:
When a model processes text, self-attention lets each word look at all other words in the sentence to build a contextual representation.

For the query word sat, the mechanism computes dot products between its query vector and the key vectors of every word.

```rh-diagram
{"version":1,"diagram":{"title":"How sat attends to the sentence","caption":"Thicker arrows carry more weight. In this example, the six weights from sat sum to 1.0.","kind":"token-links","source":["the","cat","sat","on","the","mat"],"target":["the","cat","sat","on","the","mat"],"queries":[{"index":2,"weights":[0.05,0.45,0.3,0.05,0.05,0.1]}],"normalized":true}}
```

These raw scores are scaled and passed through a softmax function to produce probabilities that sum to one. In this illustrative sentence, sat places its highest weight, 0.45, directly on cat.

This high weight captures the syntactic subject-verb bond, showing that cat matters most to sat in this specific context.

title: Attention Weights for Sat
body:
Self-attention computes how much each token focuses on others in a sequence. When the query word sat evaluates the sentence, it assigns highest importance to its surrounding context words.

```rh-diagram
{"version":1,"diagram":{"title":"How sat attends to the sentence","caption":"Thicker arrows carry more weight. In this unmasked example, the six weights from sat sum to 1.0.","kind":"token-links","source":["the","cat","sat","on","the","mat"],"target":["the","cat","sat","on","the","mat"],"queries":[{"index":2,"weights":[0.05,0.1,0.45,0.2,0.1,0.1]}],"normalized":true}}
```

Notice how the largest weight of 0.45 connects sat directly to itself, while cat receives 0.1 and on receives 0.2.

These weights are derived from dot products between vector representations, scaled and normalized using the softmax function.
